::: {.chapter-lead}
A Transformer needs an ordering signal to distinguish, for example, “the cat chases the dog” from “the dog chases the cat”. This page introduces positional mechanisms and distinguishes them from causal masking; the detailed RoPE derivation belongs in an [advanced deep dive](rope.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="The one-minute mental model"}
- **Why:** content embeddings alone do not say where a token occurs. Without positional information or an order-dependent constraint, self-attention is permutation equivariant.
- **Where:** absolute encodings are added to input representations; relative mechanisms act inside attention; **RoPE** rotates queries and keys after projection.
- **Do not conflate:** the causal mask limits which positions are visible (no future tokens), but it does not replace a mechanism that represents positions or their offsets.

**Check yourself:** can you explain why swapping two tokens must be able to change the computation, and identify where each mechanism introduces that information?
:::

## Why add positional information?

The previous page showed that lookup provides a content vector, but not the token's location in the sequence. Yet a token's role often depends on its place: swapping the order in “the cat chases the dog” can change who is chasing whom. The model therefore needs an ordering signal.

When used, the causal mask indicates which positions may be attended to (`j ≤ i`). Positional mechanisms can additionally represent an absolute position or a relative offset. These signals are complementary, not interchangeable.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why is self-attention alone not enough?"}
For content-only self-attention, with no positional bias or order-dependent mask, permuting the input rows permutes the output rows in the same way. If $P$ is a permutation matrix, then:

\[
\operatorname{Attention}(PX)=P\,\operatorname{Attention}(X).
\]

To verify this, let $S=QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$ and $A=\operatorname{softmax}(S)$, with softmax applied row-wise. For the permuted input, $Q'=PQ$, $K'=PK$, and $V'=PV$. Hence $A'=\operatorname{softmax}(PSP^\top)=PAP^\top$, and $A'V'=PAP^\top PV=PAV$.

The computation is **permutation equivariant**: it reorders its outputs along with its inputs. By itself, it therefore provides no reference that distinguishes positions in the sequence.

This property assumes that no positional signal or order-dependent constraint is present. A fixed causal mask introduces a structural ordering constraint; that role should not be confused with an explicit positional encoding.
:::

![Where positional information enters the computation: at the input for an absolute encoding, inside queries and keys for RoPE.](../images/positional-info-insertion-en.svg){fig-alt="An absolute encoding is added to the embeddings at the input, before any projection. RoPE applies rotations to queries and keys after their projections, before the QK product, so the attention scores carry positional information." width=100%}

## Three approaches to distinguish

- **Absolute encoding added to the vector:** add a position-specific vector to the token representation. The original Transformer used sinusoidal encodings; other models learn positional embeddings.
- **Relative mechanisms:** introduce the offset between positions into the attention computation, for example through a bias added to attention scores or through relative representations.
- **RoPE:** this rotary method applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys after their projections and before the \(QK^\top\) product. The resulting score depends on the relative offset. RoPE is therefore a relative-position mechanism; it is separated here to make its particular insertion point clear.

These approaches inject positional information at different points and do not have exactly the same properties. The diagram compares two explicit positional mechanisms; it does not depict the causal mask, which is a separate visibility constraint. At this stage, it is enough to understand their role and approximate location in the computation. For relative-offset dependence, rotation conventions, and long-sequence limitations, see the [advanced RoPE deep dive](rope.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Optional deepening — the geometry of sinusoidal encodings"}
In the original sinusoidal encoding, each coordinate pair uses its own frequency. Let $\omega_i=10000^{-2i/d}$. The pair associated with index $i$ is:

\[
p_i(t)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin(\omega_i t)\\
\cos(\omega_i t)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

For a fixed offset $k$, trigonometric identities give:

\[
p_i(t+k)=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(\omega_i k) & \sin(\omega_i k)\\
-\sin(\omega_i k) & \cos(\omega_i k)
\end{bmatrix}
p_i(t).
\]

Thus, a fixed offset corresponds to a fixed rotation **for a given pair and frequency**. For example, with $d=2$, the only pair has $\omega_0=1$: $p_0(0)=[0,1]^\top$ and $p_0(1)=[\sin(1),\cos(1)]^\top\approx[0.8415,0.5403]^\top$.

In this construction, $P$ is added to the embeddings at the input, $X_0=E[\text{token IDs}]+P$. This is not RoPE: RoPE rotates the projected $Q$ and $K$ after they are computed and before attention scores are formed. The geometric property above makes offsets accessible to a linear transformation; it does not guarantee that a head will actually learn a rule such as “look three tokens back”.
:::

## Common misconceptions

- **“Attention naturally knows which token comes first.”** Content-based attention does not carry that order on its own; a positional mechanism or structural constraint such as causal masking must supply it.

## Where does this step sit in the route?

The [embedding-space lookup](embedding-space.qmd) maps each ID to an initial vector that does not depend on position; this page explains why and how order is then taken into account. [Contextualized representations](contextualized-representations.qmd), the next step in the route, describe how Transformer blocks turn those initial states into context-dependent states. To go further: the [RoPE](rope.qmd) page details the rotary relative mechanism, and [causal masking](causal-masking.qmd) presents a distinct structural constraint: it orders the visible positions without encoding their positions explicitly.

- [Su et al. (2021), *RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864) — the original RoPE paper.
- [Hugging Face Transformers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/) — implementation details vary by architecture.

## Check your understanding

Formative exercises use this page in the [Transformer collection](exercises.qmd#transformer).

1. Two sentences contain the same words in a different order. Why are initial embeddings alone not enough to distinguish them?

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

The lookup assigns the same initial vector to every occurrence of a token, whatever its position. Without explicit positional information or a structural constraint, content-based attention does not carry the order on its own.

</details>

2. Does RoPE add a position vector to token embeddings?

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to the query and key vectors, after projection and before the score dot product. It is a relative mechanism, distinct from absolute encodings added to the input representations.

</details>

3. Does the causal mask replace a positional encoding?

<details>
<summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. The causal mask is a visibility constraint: it restricts each position to its prefix, imposing an order on the computation, but it encodes neither absolute positions nor relative offsets. The two mechanisms are distinct and often combined.

</details>

You have understood this step if you can explain why order must be taken into account, distinguish the three families of mechanisms, and separate explicit positional information from the causal visibility constraint.
:::
